problem: A network TV scheduler has $30$ shows to choose from to make the network's prime-time lineup of shows.  The prime-time lineup will consist of $4$ shows. How many different lineups are possible?

examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Number of Permutations of Objects Chosen From a Group of at Least Ten
examples.problem: A company has $20$ employees. A total of $4$ employees are needed to fill the roles of president, vice president, treasurer, and secretary. How many different ways can this be achieved?
examples.worked_solution:
The number of permutations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
_{n}P_r = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!}.
$$

There are $20$ employees, so $n=20.$ We want to select $4$ of those employees to fill the roles of president, vice president, treasurer, and secretary, so we have $r=4.$

Therefore, the number of different ways to fill the roles is

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{20}{P}_{4} & =\frac{20!}{(20-4)!} \\  & =\frac{20!}{16!} \\  & =\frac{20\cdot 19\cdot 18\cdot 17\cdot \cancel{16!}}{\cancel{16!}} \\  & =20\cdot 19\cdot 18\cdot 17 \\  & =116\,280.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: John couldn't recall the serial number on his new bike, but he remembered that it was $4$ digits long, each digit ranged from $0$ to $9$ and that none of the digits were used more than once. How many of these serial numbers are possible?
feedback.worked_solution:
The number of permutations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{P}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}.
$$

There are $10$ digits, so $n=10.$ We want to select $4$ of those digits for the serial number, so we have $r=4.$

Therefore, the number of different $4$-digit serial numbers is

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{10}{P}_{4} & =\frac{10!}{(10-4)!} \\  & =\frac{10!}{6!} \\  & =\frac{10\cdot 9\cdot 8\cdot 7\cdot \cancel{6!}}{\cancel{6!}} \\  & =10\cdot 9\cdot 8\cdot 7 \\  & =5\,040.\end{aligned}
$$
